description: My name is Aeyan, im really interested in robotics, astro physics and cloud computing, i am working on this project solo, im looking for team members who are willing to help expand the capabilities of our Martian mission planning software and make it more practical for real use by astronauts.
summary:
This project is a map. This project displays a map of all the discovered regions on Mars and allows astronauts or mission planners to plan walks on Mars using data from prior missions and satellites. It also displays visual imagery, 3D maps, and details such as the elevation of certain areas as well as the distances between any region on Mars.

It allows astronauts to calculate and plan routes by taking into account their capabilities: how much elevation they can climb and what speed they are traveling at. This produces a final mission plan with exact directions on which route to take, how to follow it, as well as things like distance, elevation, and the approximate time it's going to take
details:
Planning a route on Mars begins with a very human question really: what's actually between where you are and where you want to go? That's what Mars Atlas is all about. It's a website which brings together orbital imagery, topography and the locations of past missions into a single interactive map for Jezero, Gale and Gusev.

In Jezero and Gale you can pick a start point, a destination and an optional stop, set a slope limit and a range of travel assumptions. Mars Atlas then goes on to compare the various routes and will display the distance, ascent, a profile of the elevation and the heading to the various checkpoints which tells you which way to turn. You can also look at the terrain in 3D and open the source record for the data. In Gusev we currently only have imagery and the ability to measure a direct distance. We're very clear that a numerical route grid is not available there.

We hope Mars Atlas will help students, researchers and mission folks to get a real sense of the Mars data and to be more confident and inquisitive about it. It was built using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, a Web Worker, Python, NumPy and Rasterio. It uses the NASA Mars Trek imagery and the USGS terrain products derived from spacecraft observations. The Gale terrain product also incorporates data from ESA’s Mars Express. The code is on Github and the website is on Vercel, no special hardware required. Our key design decision was to have the evidence of the calculation next to the map: every route is clearly identified as a calculation with its source, resolution, assumptions and limitations all made visible. It's an exploratory research tool, not a certified navigation tool for astronauts or rovers.
